record.paper_title: Stationary solutions of the axially symmetric Einstein-Vlasov system: present status and open problems
record.original_question: Can one establish a mathematical link between nonlinear dynamical stability and the static or stationary solutions obtained by the iterative fixed-point algorithm used for Vlasov-Poisson and Einstein-Vlasov steady states?

evidence.quote: In fact there are indications that this convergent set corresponds with solutions which are dynamically stable.

A further interesting aspect of this method is related to stability. Namely, as mentioned above, there are indications that solutions obtained by this algorithm are dynamically stable. This observation is particularly exciting in view of the open problem of non-linear stability for the spherically symmetric Einstein-Vlasov system. Hence, if a link between non-linear stability and the static solutions obtained by this algorithm can be established it would certainly be of great interest.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider the spherically symmetric Vlasov–Poisson system and the spherically symmetric Einstein–Vlasov system, describing self-gravitating collisionless matter in Newtonian gravity and in general relativity, respectively. A standard procedure to construct static/stationary solutions of these systems is the following mass-preserving fixed-point iteration: starting from an initial gravitational potential (resp. metric), one defines a distribution function f as a prescribed (decreasing) function of the local particle energy (and possibly angular momentum), rescaled to keep the total ADM/Newtonian mass fixed; one then recomputes the potential (resp. metric) from f via Poisson's equation (resp. the Einstein constraints), and iterates. Numerical experiments indicate that this iteration converges to a steady state on a certain subset of microscopic equations of state, and that the steady states so obtained appear to be precisely those which are dynamically stable under the full nonlinear time evolution of the corresponding Vlasov system.

Problem: Establish a rigorous mathematical link between nonlinear dynamical stability of stationary solutions and the convergence of this iterative fixed-point algorithm. Specifically, prove (or disprove) that, for the spherically symmetric Vlasov–Poisson system and for the spherically symmetric Einstein–Vlasov system, a stationary solution arising as a fixed point to which the iteration converges is nonlinearly dynamically stable, and conversely that nonlinearly stable steady states lie in the convergence set of this algorithm.
artifact.status_search_result: Recent works (e.g., a 2024 study on Vlasov–Poisson steady states as fixed points of a mass-preserving algorithm) provide numerical and partial analytical evidence that the algorithm's convergence set coincides with dynamically stable steady states, but a rigorous mathematical link between nonlinear stability and the fixed-point iteration remains unestablished. Nonlinear stability for the spherically symmetric Einstein–Vlasov system itself is a well-known open problem, with only linear (in)stability results available.

status_evidence.title: Steady states of the spherically symmetric Vlasov-Poisson system as fixed points of a mass-preserving algorithm
status_evidence.snippet: In the relativistic case, the question whether a steady state can be obtained by this scheme seems to be related to its dynamical stability, which motivates the desire for a deeper understanding of this strategy.
status_evidence.claim: The connection between fixed-point convergence and dynamical stability is conjectural and motivates further study, not yet rigorously proven.

status_evidence.title: A Birman–Schwinger Principle in General Relativity: Linearly Stable Shells of Collisionless Matter Surrounding a Black Hole
status_evidence.snippet: Recent work proves the linear instability of certain steady states when the central redshift is sufficiently large.
status_evidence.claim: Only linear stability/instability results are available for Einstein–Vlasov; nonlinear stability remains open.
